reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: The commonest primary intraocular malignancy of childhood, usually presenting before the age of five with leukocoria or strabismus
The hereditary form is caused by a germline mutation in the RB1 tumour-suppressor gene and follows Knudson's two-hit model, with a second somatic hit initiating the tumour
Hereditary disease tends to be bilateral and multifocal and presents earlier than the sporadic, unilateral form
A germline RB1 mutation confers a substantial lifetime risk of second, non-ocular malignancies such as osteosarcoma, soft-tissue sarcoma and melanoma
The inheritance pattern is autosomal dominant with high penetrance, so genetic testing and counselling of families is essential
Diagnosis is clinical and radiological, and biopsy is avoided because of the risk of tumour seeding
Pinealoblastoma occurring with bilateral retinoblastoma is termed trilateral retinoblastoma and carries a poor prognosis
reference.pathophysiology: Retinoblastoma arises from developing retinal cells and is driven by biallelic inactivation of the RB1 tumour-suppressor gene, whose protein normally restrains cell-cycle progression. In hereditary disease one defective RB1 allele is present in every cell as a germline mutation (the first hit), and loss or mutation of the remaining functional allele within a retinal cell (the second hit) allows unregulated proliferation and tumour formation, in keeping with Knudson's two-hit hypothesis. Because the first hit is already present throughout the body, tumours tend to be bilateral and multifocal and to arise early, and the germline defect predisposes other tissues to malignancy later in life.
additionalDifferentials: Coats disease with exudative retinal detachment
Persistent fetal vasculature (persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous)
Norrie disease and other causes of a retrolental mass
Toxocariasis and other inflammatory causes of leukocoria
Congenital cataract and retinopathy of prematurity
additionalInvestigations: Examination under anaesthesia with wide-field fundus imaging to map and stage tumours
Ocular ultrasound to demonstrate an intraocular mass with characteristic calcification
MRI of the orbits and brain to assess optic nerve, extraocular spread and pineal involvement
RB1 germline molecular genetic testing with counselling and cascade screening of relatives
Surveillance examinations of at-risk siblings and offspring from infancy
redFlags: Leukocoria or new strabismus in a young child requiring urgent ophthalmology referral
A buphthalmic or painful red eye suggesting advanced intraocular disease
Signs of optic nerve or extraocular extension on imaging
New neurological symptoms or a pineal mass suggesting trilateral disease
Later bone pain or a mass in a survivor, raising concern for a second malignancy
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and modern treatment, survival from intraocular retinoblastoma is high in well-resourced settings, and eye-preserving therapy is often possible; however, patients with a germline RB1 mutation carry a lifelong increased risk of second malignancies, and extraocular or metastatic disease and trilateral retinoblastoma carry a much poorer prognosis.
pitfalls: Delaying referral of leukocoria and allowing progression to advanced disease
Performing intraocular biopsy and risking tumour dissemination
Assuming a unilateral presentation excludes a germline mutation without genetic testing
Neglecting lifelong surveillance for second malignancies in germline carriers
Failing to screen and counsel at-risk relatives
references: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
